10.1016/j.trac.2026.119107.abstract: Metabolomics provides the definitive phenotypic readout of biological systems, yet the field remains constrained by the immense complexity of chemical space, facing critical bottlenecks in data mining and the elucidation of "metabolic dark matter." As high-resolution technologies drive a shift toward high-dimensional, spatiotemporally resolved analysis, the resulting data complexity has rapidly outpaced the processing capabilities of traditional bioinformatics. To surmount these challenges, Generative Artificial Intelligence and specifically Large Language Models (LLMs) are driving a paradigm shift, elevating analytical methodologies from passive pattern recognition to proactive and deep semantic cognition. This review systematically explores how LLMs and autonomous AI agents are reshaping the entire metabolomics workflow. Under a unified “science to decision” conceptual framework, we highlight three pivotal translational pillars: (1) knowledge discovery and planning, enabling automated hypothesis generation and intelligent experimental design; (2) data-to-insight translation, focusing on spectral annotation, de novo structural prediction, and dynamic multi-omics reasoning; and (3) decision and autonomous action, integrating AI agents with robotic hardware to establish closed-loop "Self-Driving Laboratories". Finally, we critically evaluate the inherent limitations of these architectures, such as probabilistic hallucinations, physical system drift, and the "signal-to-symbol" gap. To address these challenges, we propose a strategic roadmap toward Native Mass Spectrometry Foundation Models and credible, fully autonomous AI-driven analytical chemistry.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.119107.title: The AI-driven paradigm shift in metabolomics: Large language models, autonomous agents, and self-driving laboratories

10.1016/j.trac.2026.119132.abstract: Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) is a powerful analytical technique that enables spatially resolved molecular profiling of tissues, providing insights into biological complexity. While advances in hardware and sample preparation improve MSI performance in sensitivity, spatial resolution, molecular coverage, and acquisition throughput, these gains are often constrained by trade-offs, where optimizing one metric compromises another. Computational strategies have emerged as a cost-effective means of alleviating these physicochemical trade-offs. Specifically, computational approaches can improve detection sensitivity and coverage by learning spectral and spatial patterns for signal detection, denoising, and recovery; achieve reported spatial enhancement factors of 2–20× through super-resolution reconstruction and multimodal fusion; expand annotation coverage by integrating chemical priors with learned spectral–spatial features; and accelerate acquisition through employing sparse sampling strategies followed by computational reconstruction, reducing the required number of measurements by up to 80%. This review critically examines recent computational advancements, with a focus on artificial intelligence (AI) approaches, while addressing ongoing challenges and proposing solutions. It can serve as a cross-disciplinary bridge by offering analytical chemists guidance on using computational tools to optimize the data acquisition and interpretation, and providing data scientists with MSI-specific context for developing targeted algorithms. We anticipate that advanced computational methods, particularly AI, will support next-generation MSI performance enhancement and enable new biological insights.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.119132.title: AI-driven computational enhancement of mass spectrometry imaging: Detection sensitivity, spatial resolution, molecular coverage, and acquisition throughput

10.1016/j.jag.2026.105185.abstract: Driven by global carbon neutrality initiatives, China’s rapid expansion of photovoltaic (PV) power generation necessitates large-scale and precise extraction of photovoltaic power stations (PPS) for effective resource management. However, in 10 m resolution remote sensing imagery, PPS targets frequently exhibit multi-scale and fragmented spatial distributions. Such characteristics often lead to limited model generalization, high omission rates, and elevated commission errors, particularly under sparse-sample conditions. To address these challenges, this study introduces PPS-SAM, a spectrum- and structure-aware extraction framework developed for sparse-sample scenarios based on the Segment Anything Model (SAM). PPS-SAM integrates a Spectral Enhancement Encoder to fuse near-infrared (NIR) and shortwave-infrared (SWIR) bands, thereby improving the spectral separability of PV targets from heterogeneous backgrounds. It also incorporates a High-Quality Mask Decoder to maintain edge integrity and delineate fragmented arrays more effectively. Evaluated on a newly developed 10 m multispectral PPS dataset (MSPV-Dataset), PPS-SAM demonstrated robust segmentation performance with only 11 training samples (F1: 91.47% ± 0.13%; mIoU: 91.40% ± 0.08%), notably surpassing baseline models trained on the complete 634-sample dataset. Ablation and generalization assessments indicate the effectiveness of each module in enhancing foreground detection and background suppression, with stable performance across diverse, unseen terrains and environmental disturbances (F1: 92.19%; mIoU: 92.19%). Applying this framework, nationwide PPS distribution maps for 2022 and 2024 were generated (excluding distributed rooftop systems). The results indicate that the total PPS area expanded from 3,486.41 km2 to 5,900.89 km2, representing an increase of approximately 70%. Regional analysis shows that Northwest China was characterized by predominantly centralized growth (78.77%), whereas eastern and southwestern regions exhibited significant distributed expansion. Although national spatial clustering weakened slightly (Global Moran’s I decreased from 0.4155 to 0.3112), it intensified within central and southwestern provinces. Land-use transition analysis suggests that new PV installations primarily originated from grasslands (59.04%) and barren lands (96.40%), highlighting substantial land-cover conversion. These spatio-temporal patterns underscore regional disparities in PV expansion and shifting spatial structures. This study offers a robust methodological framework for high-precision PPS identification at 10 m resolution under sparse-sample constraints, supporting efficient renewable energy management and evidence-based policy formulation. The dataset is publicly available via Figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29618429).

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118704.abstract: CRISPR-based diagnostics have expanded molecular sensing through programmable target recognition and diverse signal transduction modes, yet their analytical performance remains limited by guide RNA (gRNA) design constraints, effector variability, and heterogeneous readout formats. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer powerful solutions. Deep learning enables data-driven optimization of gRNA specificity, target interactions, and Cas protein engineering, while machine-learning models enhance automated, quantitative, and noise-tolerant interpretation of CRISPR-derived signals. Emerging methods in uncertainty estimation and explainable AI further support reliable and clinically aligned deployment. This review outlines how AI contributes across the CRISPR diagnostic workflow, accelerating Cas effector discovery and engineering, refining gRNA design and off-target assessment, and improving extraction, correction, and classification of heterogeneous output signals. Together, these developments define an emerging CRISPR-AI framework that integrates protein optimization, guide design, and signal analytics, enabling more sensitive, robust, and scalable next-generation diagnostic platforms.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118704.title: AI-enhanced CRISPR diagnostics: From gRNA design to Cas protein engineering and signal analytics

10.1016/j.trac.2025.118637.abstract: Food safety and contamination are serious global challenges because of their magnified impact on health and social well-being. Conventional detection techniques, despite their accuracy, rely on laboratory equipment, skilled operators, and time-consuming steps, which limit their use for on-site analysis. Microfluidic paper-based biosensors (μPAD-BS) have appeared as a simple, low-cost, and reliable solution for rapid food testing. Additionally, the machine learning assisted microfluidic paper-based devices have more advantages in their analytical performances and reliability. These platforms can handle complicated data, improve detection accuracy, and facilitate real-time decision-making via portable devices like smartphones when paired with machine learning. This review critically examines the integration of machine learning algorithms with μPAD-BS. It also discusses fabrication methods, algorithm selection criteria, and the trade-offs between computational cost and interpretability. It also provides insights from related fields such as biomedical diagnostics and environmental monitoring to offer scalable, ethical, and user-friendly designs. In spite of machine learning-enhanced μPAD-BS showing promising outputs, the need for further research to develop more user-oriented and intelligent sensing tools for robust food safety analysis has also been discussed in the future perspectives section.
10.1016/j.trac.2025.118637.title: Challenges in translating machine learning integrated microfluidic paper-based biosensors from lab to field: A critical analysis of scalability and socio-economic barriers

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118731.abstract: Early and accurate disease diagnosis is crucial for timely intervention and improved patient recovery. However, current diagnostic methods face significant technical challenges in enabling minimally invasive dynamic monitoring, and conventional sensors lack the ability to analyze large-scale datasets accurately and efficiently. Microneedles (MNs) technology, as a minimally invasive platform for biosensing, offers an innovative approach for biomarker monitoring when integrated with artificial intelligence (AI). Unlike existing reviews that broadly discuss AI applications in biosensing, this review focuses on the MNs biosensors, systematically analyzing material diversity, structural design innovations, and sensing mechanisms. We highlight how AI specifically address MNs-related challenges in high-dimensional biometric data processing, thereby significantly improving biosensing performance. Furthermore, we critically evaluate current bottlenecks and propose pathways for future development. This work provides a reference for the development of intelligent MNs biosensing, particularly in advancing the transformation of healthcare systems from passive detection to proactive, integrated diagnosis and treatment.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118731.title: Microneedles biosensors for disease diagnosis: From fabrication to AI enhancement

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118974.abstract: Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) combines molecular fingerprint specificity with high sensitivity and has been widely used in biomedical diagnostics, environmental monitoring, and chemical analysis. Because SERS enhancement depends on the geometry of noble metal nanostructures and the distribution of electromagnetic hotspots, small fabrication tolerances can cause large signal fluctuations that limit measurement repeatability. Discriminative machine learning methods have improved spectral interpretation but cannot directly guide substrate design. Deep generative models, together with physics-informed surrogate methods, now enable inverse design of nanostructures from target optical specifications, opening the prospect of a closed-loop between discriminative analysis and generative design for SERS substrate development. This review covers both discriminative spectral analysis and generative inverse design for SERS. We examine discriminative methods and their limitations, describe how explainable AI connects spectral analysis with structural design, and survey generative design strategies. Translational issues and future directions are also discussed.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118974.title: AI-assisted Raman spectra technique for biomedical sensing: Combine new generation of discriminative spectral analysis with generative inverse design of SERS substrate

10.1016/j.trac.2026.119030.abstract: Food safety is a global public health challenge, and the development of novel point-of-care testing (POCT) technologies with high sensitivity, high specificity, and intelligence is crucial. Optical sensing has become a research hotspot in the POCT field because of its high sensitivity and rapid response. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), with their high specific surface area, tunable pore structure, and abundant active sites, can serve as excellent optical sensing platforms. Currently, MOF-based sensing platforms can achieve highly sensitive detection of a variety of food contaminants with low detection limits, demonstrating excellent analytical performance. This review systematically summarizes the latest research progress in MOF-based artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted optical sensors for food contaminant detection. It outlines the synthesis strategies of MOFs, including solvothermal methods, in situ reduction, and post-synthetic modification, and focuses on three optical sensing mechanisms: colorimetric, fluorescence, and surface-enhanced Raman scattering. Furthermore, it highlights the deep integration of optical sensing with smartphone imaging, microfluidic arrays, and advanced machine learning algorithms in optical sensing systems. Finally, the challenges in practical applications are summarized, and the interdisciplinary development of AI-assisted MOF-based optical sensors is discussed.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.119030.title: AI-integrated MOF-based optical sensors for food contaminants: On-site, multiplex, and intelligent detection

10.1016/j.trac.2026.119093.abstract: Phenolic contaminants constitute an environmentally and biologically relevant class of pollutants due to their persistence, toxicity, and widespread occurrence in industrial effluents, food systems, and aquatic ecosystems. Reliable monitoring remains analytically challenging because of structural similarity and trace-level concentrations in complex matrices. Although various analytical approaches have been developed, achieving high selectivity in complex environmental and food samples remains difficult. In this context, molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP) sensors have emerged as promising recognition platforms, offering selective, robust, and chemically stable alternatives to biological receptors for phenolic detection. Despite these advantages, traditional MIP development still relies heavily on empirical optimization, limiting design predictability, binding-site homogeneity, and reproducibility. To facilitate the transition toward rational MIP design, computational chemistry and artificial intelligence (AI) enable molecular-level interrogation of template–monomer interactions, pre-polymerization assemblies, and binding-site architecture before experimental synthesis. Accordingly, this review critically examines recent advances in computationally guided MIP sensor development for phenolic contaminants, highlighting molecular docking, density functional theory (DFT), and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Emphasis is placed on multiscale modeling integrating electronic structure, solvent effects, and cavity dynamics to support rational imprinting. Complementing these approaches, machine learning (ML) and AI establish nonlinear structure–performance relationships from molecular descriptors, formulation variables, and experimental data, enabling monomer prioritization, formulation optimization, binding-affinity prediction, and predictive MIP design. Current challenges, including force-field accuracy, dataset scarcity, model transferability, and reproducibility, are critically discussed. Finally, future perspectives emphasize integrated digital design pipelines, hybrid physics–ML workflows, autonomous optimization, and intelligent sensing platforms for real-time phenolic monitoring.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.119093.title: Data-driven computational and machine learning design of molecularly imprinted polymer sensors for phenolic contaminants

10.1016/j.trac.2026.119146.abstract: Aptamers, as high-affinity recognition molecules, have benefited from recent advances in function-driven selection strategies and artificial intelligence-assisted discovery. However, the limited understanding of aptamer selection mechanisms often leads to target bias and stochastic outcomes, thereby hindering the reliable identification of high-performance aptamers. In complex biological environments, challenges related to reproducibility, stability, specificity, and translational robustness remain unresolved, while systematic investigations of critical physicochemical factors, including buffer composition and ionic conditions, are still lacking. This review systematically examines recent screening advances in aptamer selection technologies and the origins of target bias, summarizes current characterization and chemical modification strategies, and elucidates the key determinants governing affinity, selectivity, and specificity in practical applications. By integrating these aspects, this review provides a theoretical perspective for understanding aptamer performance, addressing major barriers to clinical translation, and facilitating the development of next-generation aptamer-based diagnostics and therapeutics.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.119146.title: The evolution of aptamer discovery: From conventional SELEX to AI-driven selection and molecular engineering

10.1016/j.trac.2025.118491.abstract: Micro(nano)plastics (MNPs) threaten terrestrial ecosystems and human health, making accurate detection and quantification crucial for risk assessment and management. Herein, this review examines current methodologies for sampling, extracting, detecting, and quantifying MNPs in soils. It summarizes recent advances in soil MNP sampling and pretreatment, including key steps like collection, sieving, drying, density separation, and organic matter removal. The review compares detection technologies such as visual identification, vibrational spectroscopy, and mass spectrometry, highlighting their advantages and limitations. Special emphasis is placed on the emerging use of AI-driven methods for automated, standardized, and high-throughput MNP identification and quantification. The review also discusses current quantification strategies and identifies key research needs and opportunities in this field, aiming to guide future research on soil MNP detection and assessment. Overall, this review consolidates current advances and outlines key challenges to guide future research on soil MNP detection and assessment.
10.1016/j.trac.2025.118491.title: Micro(nano)plastic detection in soils: analytical techniques, AI applications, and future challenges

10.1016/j.trac.2025.118520.abstract: Biosensors have become indispensable tools in healthcare, environmental monitoring, and biotechnology, with their performance critically dependent on interfacial chemistry and surface functionalization strategies. This review looks closely at recent advances in surface modification methods to enhance biosensor sensitivity and selectivity. The significant functionalization strategies addressed in this work include covalent and non-covalent immobilization procedures, along with novel nanomaterial-based enhancements that increase signal transmission and biorecognition precision. The fundamentals of surface interactions, biomolecule stability, and the shortcomings of conventional functionalization techniques are critically discussed. The primary focus is on the revolutionary effects of artificial intelligence (AI) in interfacial chemistry, where computational modelling and machine learning are transforming material design, property prediction, and biosensor optimization. The recent advancements at the convergence of AI, nanotechnology, and synthetic biology, which facilitate the development of intelligent biosensing platforms, are highlighted. A paradigm shift in biosensor development is represented by the use of AI models for functional material analysis, which provide data-driven answers to surface characterization challenges. Furthermore, the ethical issues and technical challenges related to AI-driven biosensor development are also covered, including data bias, repeatability, and sustainable production. This review systematically covers research activities during 2018–2025, providing a comprehensive overview of surface functionalization strategies, nanomaterial enhancements, and AI-driven approaches for biosensor development. Also, the review paper offers a roadmap for overcoming present constraints and opening up new possibilities in high-performance sensing technologies by combining interdisciplinary advancements in surface chemistry, nanotechnology, and AI.
10.1016/j.trac.2025.118520.title: AI-enhanced surface functionalization in biosensors: From fundamentals to future prospects

10.1016/j.trac.2025.118536.abstract: Emerging contaminants (ECs), characterized by diverse structures, low environmental concentrations, and complex mixture effects, challenge conventional toxicity screening. Traditional approaches face limitations in efficiency, costs, and handling large datasets. Deep learning (DL) offers a transformative tool for predicting ECs toxicity by leveraging feature learning and nonlinear modeling. DL significantly enhance prediction accuracy while reducing time and economic costs compared to conventional techniques. This review systematically examines advancements in DL applications for ECs toxicity screening in two key areas: data requirements and preprocessing, as well as innovative algorithmic architectures and optimized mechanisms. It highlights the superior performance of advanced architectures like Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Transformers in processing molecular graphs and capturing long-range dependencies. Furthermore, we analyze core technical challenges, including data scarcity, interpretability issues, and limited knowledge of environmental interactions, and suggest future directions to guide the practical application of DL in environmental risk assessment.
10.1016/j.trac.2025.118536.title: Deep learning-driven screening of emerging contaminants: Innovations and technological advances

10.1016/j.trac.2025.118603.abstract: Terahertz bioeffects in neurobiology research have developed fast in the last two decades. Numerous theoretical calculations based on proteins and molecules are performed in order to clarify the intricate principles of molecular dynamics as well as the interactions between cells and terahertz radiation. At this stage of science, interdisciplinary research has obvious advantages in studying the processes of terahertz radiation regulating molecular conformation, modulating neuroelectrophysiology, enhancing the dynamic changes of synaptic plasticity, and intervening in neurodegenerative diseases. This paper focuses on the latest advancements in the interaction between terahertz radiation and the nervous system in terms of molecules, cells, synapses, and pathologies. It evaluates the influence, efficacy, mechanism of action, and application methods of terahertz exposure in-vitro and in-vivo on neuronal excitability, synaptic transmission, neurogenesis, cognitive function, and behavioral phenotypes. The dependence of different neurobiological effects on specific terahertz radiation parameters is also an aspect that cannot be ignored.
10.1016/j.trac.2025.118603.title: Neurobiological effects and mechanisms of terahertz radiation: From molecular interactions to neural function modulation

10.1016/j.trac.2025.118592.abstract: In recent years, biosensing technologies have gained increasing attention for their roles in health monitoring and disease diagnosis. However, challenges such as complex background noise and signal analysis limit their broader application. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), shows strong promise to address these issues. This review overviews widely used traditional ML algorithms and deep learning models in biosensing, summarizing advances in neural network architectures and highlighting techniques such as data augmentation, fusion, and transfer learning that support model optimization for biosensing tasks. We further examine AI applications in electrochemical, colorimetric, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), and fluorescence sensing, focusing on recent progress in health monitoring, disease diagnosis, short-term glucose prediction, and virtual fluorescence staining. Finally, we discuss the challenges of integrating ML into biosensing and offer perspectives on potential solutions, aiming to provide valuable guidance for the future development of AI-driven biosensing technologies.
10.1016/j.trac.2025.118592.title: Advances and challenges in the application of artificial intelligence to medical biosensing technology: A review

10.1016/j.trac.2025.118645.abstract: Terahertz sensing techniques have been widely utilized to determine the properties of targets across a range of fields in recent years. Artificial intelligence algorithms provide a promising solution to address the escalating need for higher efficiency and accuracy. With the aid of artificial intelligence algorithms, terahertz sensing techniques can significantly improve their performance in terms of analytical sensitivity, imaging resolution, and operational efficacy. This review is devoted to the recent advances in terahertz sensing techniques assisted by artificial intelligence algorithms. First, an overview of terahertz sensing techniques and artificial intelligence algorithms is provided. Subsequently, the applications of artificial intelligence algorithms in terahertz spectroscopy, imaging, and metasensor design are elaborated in detail. Finally, a conclusion and outlook for artificial intelligence algorithms-assisted terahertz sensing techniques are presented.
10.1016/j.trac.2025.118645.title: Recent advances in application of artificial intelligence algorithms in terahertz sensing techniques

10.1016/j.trac.2025.118644.abstract: Bioimaging, along with embryology is being reshaped by next-generation imaging and analytical technologies. Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM), as a leading next-generation technique, provides high-resolution, three-dimensional imaging of embryos over time, surpassing traditional methods such as confocal microscopy, widefield fluorescence microscopy, and Raman microscopy. LSFM has significantly diminished phototoxicity and enabled rapid imaging of entire embryo volumes, enhancing our ability to investigate early-to mid-embryonic development from fertilization through organogenesis in both human and animal models. In parallel with these imaging advancements, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven examination of embryo metabolism is transforming the evaluation of embryo quality and viability, as metabolic activity reflects the embryo's developmental competence and health status. This review analyzes the convergence of LSFM and AI-driven metabolic profiling as a transformative change in reproductive One Health. By integrating next-generation bioimaging into the One Health paradigm, we emphasize its potential to connect fundamental discoveries with cross-species applications in reproductive health.
10.1016/j.trac.2025.118644.title: Next-generation bioimaging in reproductive One Health: Light sheet fluorescence microscopy and AI-driven embryo metabolism analysis

10.1016/j.trac.2025.118642.abstract: Electrochemical technology has emerged as a highly promising approach for diverse advanced applications, including energy conversion, substance detection, chemical synthesis, and precision machining. Its recent application in molecular diagnosis is particularly significant, as it enables monitoring of molecular-level changes and provides dynamic feedback during biological processes. In neurological medicine, the primary role of electrochemical molecular diagnostics lies in recording in situ fluctuations of neurochemicals. Moreover, various electrochemical techniques and sensors serve as indispensable tools in molecular diagnostic workflows and have been increasingly applied to neurological applications. This review highlights the technical advances in electrochemical technologies for molecular diagnostics reported in the past five years. We further discuss the current limitations and future challenges associated with the clinical translation of electrochemical neural biosensors, with particular emphasis on their potential for rapid high-throughput screening of large-scale clinical samples and real-time in vivo detection.
10.1016/j.trac.2025.118642.title: From laboratory development to clinical translation: Electrochemical sensing strategy for neural interfaces

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118702.abstract: Cervical cancer remains a major global health challenge, particularly in low-resource settings. This review highlights next-generation point-of-care tests leveraging programmable biorecognition elements — such as aptamers, nanobodies, peptide nucleic acids, and CRISPR-Cas systems — for sensitive detection of HPV and host biomarkers. Integrated with nanomaterials, microfluidics, and smartphone-AI readouts, these biosensors enable rapid, affordable, and field-deployable screening. However, translating analytical breakthroughs into population-level impact requires overcoming critical translational barriers—including cost, tropical stability, self-sampling compatibility, and integration into fragmented health systems. We argue that future innovation must shift from performance-centric to equity-centered design, co-developed with end-users in high-burden regions. We critically assess design strategies, clinical translation potential, and implementation pathways, emphasizing equitable access aligned with the WHO's cervical cancer elimination initiative and the One Health vision.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118702.title: Next-generation point-of-care diagnostics for cervical cancer: Integrating programmable biorecognition, nanomaterials, and artificial intelligence

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118665.abstract: Antibiotics play a vital role in veterinary and human medicine for combating infectious diseases and maintaining animal health. In dairy farming, antimicrobials are widely used for therapeutic and preventive purposes, including dry-cow therapy and medicated milk replacers for calves. While these practices are essential for livestock welfare and economic sustainability, they may result in antibiotic residues in milk and derived products. Infants are particularly vulnerable to such residues due to rapid development, immature detoxification systems, and distinct exposure patterns. Consequently, the detection and control of antibiotic residues in infant milk formula (IMF) are of critical importance to public health. IMF is a fortified matrix rich in proteins and lipids, with added carbohydrates and minerals, which can induce stronger matrix effects and analyte–matrix interactions than regular milk. These characteristics require IMF-specific extraction and cleanup strategies, such as fat removal, protein precipitation, and chelation steps, to ensure accurate ultra-trace quantification. This review presents the first analysis of advanced analytical workflows developed over the past 10 years for the separation and quantification of antibiotic residues in IMF. Particular emphasis is placed on sample preparation approaches tailored to the complex IMF matrix and on chromatographic separation techniques, including high-performance liquid chromatography, ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography, and hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography. In addition, this review highlights the growing role of chemometrics and artificial intelligence-driven platforms in enhancing data interpretation and predicting contamination risks. By integrating analytical chemistry, food safety, and computational intelligence, this review provides a timely reference for researchers, regulators, and industry professionals worldwide.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118665.title: Ultra-trace detection of antibiotic residues in infant milk formula: Advanced analytical and AI-assisted approaches

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118703.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) materials enable field-effect transistor (FET) with atomic-scale channels, high carrier mobility, and strongly surface-dominated conduction, offering powerful platforms for biosensing and analysis. However, translating high-dimensional yet complex electrical signals from 2D material-based FET (2D FET) into reliable analytical outputs and decisions remains challenging. Machine learning (ML) provides a principled framework to handle non-linear responses, device-to-device variability, and high-dimensional datasets arising from multichannel and time-resolved measurements. This review introduces the principles of 2D FET sensing, including material/device architectures, transduction mechanisms, and key performance metrics. The integration of ML in 2D material design, device fabrication, and signal analytics is also discussed. Recent advances in biosensing small molecules, nucleic acids, proteins, neuromorphic activities and clinically health models are summarized. Key challenges in materials processing, interface chemistry, signal analytics, and translational deployment are finally discussed, underscoring the significance of integrating ML algorithms with advanced 2D FET sensors for next-generation health-care systems.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118703.title: Machine-learning assisted 2D field-effect transistors for intelligent biosensing and analysis
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118703.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118748.abstract: Terahertz (THz) technology, renowned for its unique molecular fingerprint recognition ability and penetration properties, holds revolutionary potential in agricultural field. However, THz data analysis faces significant challenges, including high-dimensional datasets and complex feature extraction. Artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms have emerged as transformative tools to overcome these limitations. Unlike previous reviews on THz technology or chemometric methods in agriculture, this work systematically reviews AI-driven THz data analysis across six core agricultural domains: foreign object detection, transgenic crop recognition, variety identification, quality evaluation, component analysis, and detection of hazardous substances/pesticide residues. This review analysis reveals that AI-enhanced frameworks consistently surpass conventional methods. In optimized scenarios, deep learning-enhanced models have demonstrated accuracy levels as high as 95%-100%, marking a 12%-25% improvement over chemometric approaches. Crucially, this work highlights the AI-THz paradigm that bridges lab-grade precision with scalable farm monitoring. It provides a strategic roadmap for sustainable farming, filling a critical Agri-Tech literature gap.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118748.title: Intelligent terahertz data analysis in agriculture: A systematic review of AI-driven approaches
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118748.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118741.abstract: Deep learning (DL) is driving a transition from expert-dependent chemometrics paradigm to a data-driven intelligent paradigm. This review summarizes DL progress in spectral analysis, covering the entire process from preprocessing and feature extraction to qualitative and quantitative modeling. It introduces representative DL architectures, such as convolutional neural network (CNN), recurrent neural network (RNN), generative adversarial network (GAN), and Transformer. It also elaborates on the applications of these architectures to various spectroscopic techniques, such as ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy, near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, terahertz spectroscopy, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy, and hyperspectral imaging. Furthermore, it explores critical frontier technologies such as explainable AI, multispectral fusion, and transfer learning. The discussion extends to current data-level and model-level challenges, including label scarcity, generalization limits, and deployment constraints. Finally, future research directions are proposed, highlighting the transition of spectral analysis towards an autonomous, robust, and interpretable paradigm.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118741.title: Advances in deep learning for intelligent non-destructive spectral analysis: From preprocessing and data augmentation to interpretability, fusion, and transfer learning
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118741.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118740.abstract: Fungal infection in fresh fruits (FIFF) causes quality and quantity loss, posing potential health risks and economic loss, respectively. Since it occurs asymptomatically in postharvest stages, its detection, quantification, and monitoring cause mistaken-prone and time-consuming visual observation and manual handling. Recent advancements in computer vision (ComV) technologies, alongside non-destructive imaging and non-imaging spectroscopic technologies, have enabled the real-time investigation of disease detection in fruits. Therefore, the synergistic integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with spectroscopic techniques is revolutionizing the quantification, characterization and detection of FIFF by rapid, non-destructive and data driven analysis. Thus, this article particularly synthesizes the recent applications of advanced spectroscopic techniques, ComV, and AI-driven (machine learning, deep learning) approaches for quantification of FIFF. Additionally, highlights how imaging and AI-driven techniques depict the strong potential for real-time detection and severity estimation of fungal contamination. These offer solutions to the limitations of traditional methods, which are often prone to error, destructive, and labor-intensive. Future research is expected to focus on integrating techniques with optimized algorithms and implementing them within assembly lines for enhanced commercial value.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118740.title: AI and spectroscopy synergy: Revolutionizing fungal infection detection in fresh fruits for enhanced quality control
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118740.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118784.abstract: Behavioral analysis is pivotal for understanding insect ecological functions and stress responses. Recently, microplastics have emerged as widespread contaminants capable of inducing biologically significant behavioral alterations, even at sub-lethal levels. However, detecting these fine-scale effects remains challenging for conventional ecotoxicological methods that rely on coarse endpoints like mortality. This review synthesizes current knowledge on microplastic impacts and critiques traditional assessment limitations. Furthermore, we highlight how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping behavioral ecotoxicology through advanced bioimage analysis, including machine vision tracking and deep-learning pose estimation (e.g., DeepLabCut, SLEAP). These computational approaches function as digital biosensing tools, facilitating the ultrasensitive detection of subtle changes in movement dynamics. By integrating AI, researchers can achieve higher sensitivity and throughput, strengthening behavioral endpoints within the One Health framework. Finally, we outline future directions for applying AI to quantify microplastic-induced behavioral effects in insects.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118784.title: Assessing microplastic impacts on insect behaviour through artificial intelligence tools
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118784.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118774.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) and organic pollutants (OPs) commonly coexist in the environment. In aquatic environments, the adsorption of OPs onto MPs can increase the ecological risks associated with MP pollution. The multifaceted interactions between MPs and OPs are complex, making traditional manual analysis both time-consuming and labor-intensive. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) offers powerful tools to address these challenges by rapidly processing large datasets and uncovering hidden patterns. This review focused on the transformative role of AI in advancing our understanding of MPs adsorbing OPs. We outlined the key stages in AI model development—including data collection, preprocessing, algorithm selection, and model evaluation—with the aim of improving insights into MPs–OPs interactions. Furthermore, we critically evaluated recent research progress, assessed the capacity of AI methods to unravel complex adsorption mechanisms and influencing factors, and discussed prevailing challenges. Finally, we proposed directions for future research to overcome these limitations.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118774.title: Application of artificial intelligence in unveiling the adsorption of organic pollutants by microplastics in aquatic environments: Status, challenges, and perspectives
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118774.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118782.abstract: Recent advances in soft nanomaterials, electrochemical biosensing, and flexible neural implants are redefining approaches to neurodegenerative disease diagnostics. Traditional imaging methods such as PET, SPECT, and MRI have enabled early detection of pathological changes but face limitations due to cost, accessibility, and sensitivity. Emerging biosensors, optical and electrochemical, enhanced with nanomaterials, offer portable, real-time, and minimally invasive alternatives for detecting key biomarkers including protein aggregates, neurotransmitters, and inflammatory signals. Flexible implants utilizing conductive polymers, carbon-based nanomaterials, and nanocomposites address mechanical mismatch and chronic stability issues, ensuring sustained performance within neural tissue. Innovations such as wireless, biodegradable implants further expand possibilities for continuous, personalized monitoring. This review highlights the convergence of materials science, neurobiology, and bioelectronics toward a transformative future in early diagnosis and therapeutic management of neurodegenerative diseases.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118782.title: Advances in neurodegenerative disease diagnosis: from conventional techniques to soft nanomaterial-enabled electrochemical neural implants
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118782.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118824.abstract: The technological progress over the time has enabled the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet-of-Things (IoT) with nanotechnology, making a paradigm shift in the realm of sensing and catalytic management of hazardous substances such as water contaminants, airborne particulates, and soil-based toxins. In contrast to conventional laboratory-centric analytical approaches with a resource-intensive and time-consuming nature, it is significant to develop advanced monitoring systems for real-time detection and predictive capabilities. This review explores green nanomaterials-based modern sensors and catalysts for the detection and management of hazardous substances in different environments, i.e., water, air, and soil, along with fuel generation. Life cycle assessment (LCA) approaches are significant for evaluating and guiding the development of green nanomaterials. The integration of sustainable nano-enabled sensors and catalysts with artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) systems is also deliberated. The convergence of these technologies can help in overcoming the complexities in the detection and management of pollutants occurring due to the dynamic nature of the environment. This study seeks to empower humans, stakeholders, and pollution monitoring industries through rapid sensing and predictive analysis on the basis of sensor-generated informatics using AIoT. The analysis of AIoT informatics can help in the possible risk assessment of pollutants and optimization of necessary safety measures. Finally, the real-world limitations of sustainable nanotechnology-enabled AIoT systems are discussed with significant emphasis on associated challenges and potential progress.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118824.title: Integration of sustainable nanotechnology with artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) for environmental applications
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118824.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118899.abstract: Microfluidic technologies and paper-based analytical devices are increasingly expected to deliver laboratory-grade decisions from microliter samples, often under field conditions rather than controlled environments. This demand exposes a central bottleneck: signals are multiplexed and noisy, device-to-device variation is consequential, and manual readout cannot scale. Artificial intelligence and machine learning address these limits by linking platform design, data generation, and inference into a single development loop—the organizing principle of this review. Device architecture and materials selection are discussed alongside data-efficient optimization of channel geometry, droplet operations, and digital actuation. Scenario-specific pipelines are then synthesized for image-based readout, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy decoding, and electrochemical or impedance quantification, with emphasis placed on calibration and distribution-shift performance instead of single-cohort accuracy. Biomedical diagnostics and biological analysis are treated as demanding proving grounds, where automated readout and robustness determine whether performance translates beyond demonstration. Deployment is positioned as an upfront design requirement rather than an afterthought. Accordingly, edge-capable inference, disciplined benchmarking, dataset governance, and tamper-evident provenance are treated as practical prerequisites for translation. In combination, these elements move microdevices beyond passive hardware and toward intelligent analytical systems that deliver reproducible, decision-ready evidence.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118899.title: From passive chips to intelligent platforms: AI-enabled design, control, and signal decoding in microfluidic and paper-based analytical devices
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118899.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118856.abstract: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) faces critical bottlenecks in quality control and efficacy validation due to its complex matrices and subjective traditional evaluation methods. By benchmarking 116 high-impact studies (2010–2025), this review highlights a strategic transition from shallow-learning pattern recognition to cognitive knowledge reasoning, facilitated by Large Language Models (LLMs) and Explainable AI (XAI). Although deep learning architectures achieve superior accuracies (up to 100%) across modalities like HPLC and SERS, cognitive intelligence remains essential for decoding TCM's non-linear pharmacological networks. Synthesizing “medicine-food homology” with multi-modal data fusion, we elucidate a paradigm shift from empirical practices to mechanism-interpretable precision therapies. Ultimately, this work provides a technical roadmap for AIoT-driven quality-by-design, offering a systematic blueprint to harmonize international standards and accelerate the global integration of the TCM industry.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118856.title: Empowering Traditional Chinese Medicine with artificial intelligence: Innovations in quality control, therapeutic applications, and industrialization
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118856.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118965.abstract: Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) has emerged as an important molecular sensing platform for biomedical analysis owing to its high sensitivity, chemical specificity, and label-free detection capability. When coupled with artificial intelligence (AI), SERS enables automated spectral processing, feature extraction, and pattern recognition in complex biological systems. However, most current SERS–AI studies still rely primarily on single spectrum inputs, which provide only limited information about the biochemical heterogeneity of clinical samples and may thereby constrain model robustness, interpretability, and generalizability. This review examines the development of SERS–AI from an information dimensionality perspective and highlights its conceptual evolution from single-spectrum analysis toward multidimensional information integration. We first discuss SERS enhancement mechanisms, substrate design, and AI-assisted spectral analysis, followed by a summary of representative biomedical applications of single-spectrum SERS–AI, including cancer screening, pathogen identification, disease diagnosis, pharmaceutical analysis, and therapeutic monitoring. We then discuss the transition from information-limited analysis to high-dimensional integrated diagnosis, as well as the new challenges introduced by this shift. Particular emphasis is placed on multispectral and multimodal SERS–AI strategies. Multispectral approaches, including multi-substrate, multi-excitation wavelength, and multi-biofluid, expand information dimensionality within the SERS domain, whereas multimodal approaches integrate SERS with orthogonal information from fluorescence/infrared spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, omics, imaging, or clinical data. Furthermore, we discuss data fusion strategies, validation issues, standardization requirements, and interpretability challenges, all of which are critical for advancing the clinical translation of SERS–AI. Finally, we outline future directions for developing reliable, robust, and clinically translatable SERS–AI platforms for precision biomedical analysis.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118965.title: SERS–AI for biomedical applications: From single spectrum to multidimensional analysis
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118965.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118970.abstract: Point-of-care testing (POCT) has revolutionized clinical diagnostics, enabling rapid and decentralized testing closer to the patient. While analytical performance has significantly improved, transforming lab-developed prototypes into clinically validated, market-ready devices remains a persistent obstacle. This review explores the current POCT landscape using the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) framework, highlighting key barriers that slow progress from proof-of-concept (TRL 3–4) to real-world validation (TRL 5–6) and full clinical deployment (TRL 7–9). Machine learning-driven data analysis and life cycle assessment work together as interconnected enablers for successful translation, while physics-informed neural networks are examined as a promising but early-stage direction currently at TRL 3–4. By mapping these barriers and enablers within the TRL framework, this review outlines a structured, actionable roadmap for developing POCT systems that simultaneously meet clinical efficacy, regulatory compliance, and environmental sustainability standards, reframing these not as competing priorities but as mutually reinforcing pillars of responsible diagnostic innovation.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118970.title: Bridging the POCT valley of death: An integrated roadmap for regulatory compliance, sustainability, and machine learning
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118970.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118913.abstract: Seed vigor serves as a critical determinant of crop establishment and yield stability, yet conventional vigor assessment methods remain destructive, time-consuming, and labor-intensive. In response, the field is undergoing a paradigm shift toward non-destructive detection (NDD) techniques, which integrate advanced spectroscopy, imaging modalities, and artificial intelligence (AI) for rapid and scalable evaluation. This review introduces the Vigor Signal Mechanism (VSM) model as a solution to the “black box” nature of AI-driven seed vigor predictions. This model elucidates how biochemical and structural deteriorations manifest as measurable spectral and imaging features. By mapping sensor responses to established vigor indicators, the VSM framework enhances the biological interpretability of AI models and guides the rational selection of sensing modalities. This review systematically synthesizes recent advances in spectroscopy/imaging technologies, including near-infrared spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, terahertz sensing, multispectral imaging, hyperspectral imaging, machine vision, magnetic resonance imaging, X-ray radiography, and their confluence with AI-driven analytical frameworks for seed vigor prediction. We further underscore the inherent limitations of unimodal approaches and the crucial role of multimodal information in effectively augmenting model performance. By bridging seed physiology, sensing physics, and AI, this work provides a systematic theoretical and technical reference for the academic research of seed vigor non-destructive detection, and lays a foundation for the industrialization of high-throughput, mechanism-aware seed phenotyping systems.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118913.title: A vigor signal mechanism framework guided non-destructive detection of seed vigor: Integrating spectroscopy, imaging, and artificial intelligence
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118913.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118986.abstract: Microfibers have emerged as environmental pollutants of increasing concern because of their widespread sources, persistence, confusion with natural fibers, and ecological and health risks. Detection techniques, including microscopic imaging, vibrational spectroscopy, and hyperspectral imaging, are important for microfiber identification, characterization, and analysis. However, complex environmental matrices and background interference still cause poor signal quality, low throughput, and limited adaptability. Artificial intelligence (AI), with strong nonlinear feature extraction and pattern recognition capabilities, offers a feasible solution. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-assisted microfiber detection, compares traditional machine-learning and deep-learning models, outlines relevant neural network architectures, and discusses strategies such as data augmentation, multimodal fusion, and transfer learning. We further review AI applications in microscopic imaging, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) and Raman spectroscopy, and hyperspectral imaging, focusing on identification, segmentation, counting, and polymer classification, and discuss future opportunities and challenges.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118986.title: Artificial intelligence-powered imaging of microfibers: Microscopy, vibrational and hyperspectral analysis
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118986.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118992.abstract: Water quality deterioration rarely manifests as a sudden collapse; it is more often a gradual accumulation of deviations. Changes in ion balance, trace organic matter content, or microbial dynamics are particularly difficult to detect routinely, yet they continuously create ecological stress. These signals are often too subtle for routine spot sampling or network-level surveillance, so reliable detection may occur only after regulatory or ecological thresholds have already been exceeded. Microdevice technologies are reshaping how such analytical gaps are approached. In microfluidic platforms, fluid transport, chemical reactions, and signal transduction are intrinsically co-localized, allowing rapid extraction of chemical information from minimal sample volumes with reduced latency. Microfluidic paper-based analytical devices advance this paradigm by eliminating external pumping and fixed infrastructure, relocating measurement directly to sites of concern. Integrated high-performance sensors increase both sensitivity and temporal resolution without compromising operational simplicity, even in chemically heterogeneous aquatic systems. Accordingly, microfluidic devices, paper-based platforms, and high-performance sensor hybrids are considered here as complementary—rather than competing—strategies for aquatic monitoring. Moreover, recent advances in materials science, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence (AI) have significantly expanded their analytical performance, robustness, and data interpretation capability. Device architectures, material functions, and sensing mechanisms are examined across analyte classes spanning nutrients, toxic metals, pathogens, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, emerging micropollutants, and microbial indicators. This review provides a comprehensive survey of the technologies of microdevices, their working principles, representative applications, and performance characteristics. Particular attention is given to challenges related to stability, scalability, selectivity, and real-world deployment, as well as emerging solutions. Finally, the growing role of AI in signal processing, pattern recognition, and predictive modeling is examined, and future perspectives for intelligent, autonomous water monitoring systems are proposed.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118992.title: Intelligent microdevices for aquatic monitoring: High-Performance sensing integration and AI-enabled signal decoding
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118992.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.118982.abstract: Odor sensing using colorimetric sensor arrays (CSAs) provides a rapid, low-cost, and non-destructive strategy for food safety and quality evaluation. However, practical deployment of conventional CSAs is constrained by limited stability, humidity tolerance, and reproducibility, while conventional chemometric methods often struggle with complex gas mixtures. Recent advances in nanomaterial-enabled sensor engineering have improved CSA performance, while spectroscopic and imaging approaches enable more information-rich and often high-dimensional readouts with complementary chemical and spatial information. AI offers flexible tools for high-dimensional data via feature learning, dimensionality reduction, and predictive modeling. This review provides an integrated synthesis of AI-assisted CSAs (CSAs-AI) across sensor engineering, high-dimensional readouts, AI-based modeling, and food-monitoring applications. Sensing mechanisms, fabrication strategies, spectroscopic techniques and advanced imaging methods are summarized, with emphasis on how deep learning improves qualitative and quantitative analysis of high-dimensional responses. Representative applications, current deployment bottlenecks, and future directions are also highlighted.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118982.title: Advances in AI-assisted odor sensing using colorimetric sensor arrays: From sensor design to high-dimensional data intelligence
10.1016/j.trac.2026.118982.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.119029.abstract: Electrochemical biosensors have emerged as powerful analytical platforms for the early detection and monitoring of skin cancer biomarkers owing to their high sensitivity, rapid response, miniaturization, and compatibility with point-of-care diagnostics. However, their clinical translation remains limited by biofouling, signal drift, interfacial instability, matrix interference, and poor long-term reproducibility. Beyond biomolecular recognition, biosensor performance is governed by interfacial electrochemistry, electron-transfer kinetics, mass transport, and signal transduction, which collectively determines signal generation, amplification, and analytical reliability. This review critically examines these physicochemical processes from a mechanistic and systems-level perspective. Emphasis is placed on clinically relevant biomarkers for melanoma and selected non-melanoma skin cancers, including proteins, nucleic acids, extracellular vesicles, and metabolic markers, together with challenges arising from biomarker heterogeneity, low abundance, and complex biological matrices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for electrochemical data analysis is evaluated, highlighting advances in feature extraction, pattern recognition, predictive modeling, and decision support, as well as limitations related to data quality, overfitting, interpretability, and clinical generalizability. Emerging AI-assisted electrochemical theranostic systems are discussed as closed-loop platforms integrating biomarker sensing, data-driven analysis, and therapeutic actuation for personalized disease management. Finally, key barriers to clinical translation, including standardization, validation, regulatory requirements, wearable and minimally invasive sensing technologies, and skin cancer-specific therapeutic delivery, are assessed. By integrating electrochemical sensing principles, AI-driven analytics, and translational considerations, this review provides a systems-oriented framework for developing reliable, intelligent, and clinically viable electrochemical biosensing platforms for next-generation skin cancer diagnosis and theranostics.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.119029.title: AI-driven electrochemical biosensing platforms for skin cancer: Analytical advances toward intelligent theranostic and drug-delivery systems
10.1016/j.trac.2026.119029.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.119023.abstract: Mass spectrometry (MS) is one of the most powerful tools in environmental analysis due to its excellent analytical performance. Recently, the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has brought new research paradigms and efficiency revolution to environmental MS, significantly accelerating methodology development, optimizing process management, and breaking the bottleneck of complex data analysis. This review aims to introduce the advances of GenAI approaches, emphasizing their features, advantages, and limitations in environmental MS analysis. The significant applications of GenAI in sample preparation methodology and MS data process are highlighted. The opportunities and challenges for further development of GenMS are also discussed.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.119023.title: Generative AI for environmental mass spectrometry: Opportunities and challenges
10.1016/j.trac.2026.119023.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.trac.2026.119021.abstract: Seed vigor is a crucial agronomic trait that strongly influences crop establishment, agricultural productivity, and global food security. Conventional detection methods are often destructive, time-consuming, and subjective, and they frequently fail to capture internal biochemical deterioration within seeds. This review first clarifies the major physiological and biochemical factors affecting seed vigor, including membrane integrity, reserve metabolism, oxidative damage, enzyme activity, moisture status, and embryo integrity. It then systematically summarizes advanced non-destructive technologies for seed vigor assessment, including near-infrared, Raman, terahertz, fluorescence, and photoacoustic spectroscopy, as well as hyperspectral imaging, X-ray imaging, and biospeckle laser techniques. Multi-spectral fusion strategies are also discussed, as they integrate complementary physical and chemical information to improve detection sensitivity and robustness. Methodologically, this review highlights the integration of spectral data with chemometrics, machine learning, and deep learning for qualitative classification and quantitative prediction of seed vigor. As data-driven models become increasingly complex, algorithm interpretability has become a key concern. Therefore, this review further analyzes how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods help address the “black box” problem, verify model reliability, and reveal links between spectral features and physiological mechanisms such as lipid peroxidation and protein denaturation. Overall, coupling molecular spectroscopy with interpretable intelligent algorithms can enhance detection accuracy, robustness, and generalization, providing technical support for high-throughput seed quality management and precision agriculture.
10.1016/j.trac.2026.119021.title: Application of spectroscopic techniques with machine learning for high-throughput phenotyping of seed vigor: A comprehensive review
